name: Bloodstone
spiritual: Roots you in the physical world
physical: Traditionally linked to vitality and stamina
Associated with a sense of circulation of energy
Often carried by people who want extra strength on demanding days
summary: Bloodstone is the dark green chalcedony flecked with red, an old warrior's talisman for courage, vitality and grounding. Learn its lore and care.
intro: Bloodstone is a dark green, opaque chalcedony scattered with spots of brick-red or orange iron oxide, which look like drops of blood on moss. The green comes from tiny inclusions of chlorite or other green minerals, and the red from hematite. Some pieces carry only a few red freckles, others are heavily splashed. It polishes to a good shine, so you meet it as cabochons, signet rings, tumbled stones and carved seals. Compared with showier gems it looks modest at first glance, then keeps drawing you back with its deep forest tone.
history: The old name heliotrope means sun turner, from a belief that the stone could make the sun turn red or even darken it. A medieval legend says bloodstone formed when the blood of Christ fell on green jasper at the foot of the cross. That story made it popular for religious carvings, especially of the Passion. Roman soldiers and later knights wore it for strength, and some folklore said it could stop bleeding, a claim that belongs to tradition only. Bloodstone is the traditional March birthstone, a rival to aquamarine, and mining centers in India still supply much of it.
meaning: In crystal lore bloodstone is the stone of courage, endurance and renewal. Healers connect it to the root chakra for its grounding strength and to the heart chakra for the blood-red flecks. People carry it when they need stamina and nerve, whether that is for training, a long shift, or standing up for someone else. It is said to calm irritable moods and clear stagnant energy from a space. Because of the red-and-green symbolism, many see it as balancing action with compassion. Some traditions call it a stone of luck for athletes and for people in pursuit of difficult goals. It is considered best for steady commitment rather than quick thrills.
howToUse: Carry a tumbled bloodstone in a pocket during demanding days or workouts. Wear it as a ring or pendant for ongoing courage, or set a polished piece by the entrance of your home as a guard. Hold it in meditation with a hand on the lower belly and breathe slowly, picturing green and red light rooting you. A small stone placed on a desk supports long hours of study or labor. Pair it with a heart-opening stone like rose quartz if you want courage that stays kind.
care: Bloodstone is hard and tolerates water, so a quick wash with mild soap is fine. Cleanse it with smoke, sound, running water or a rest on selenite. It handles sunlight and moonlight well, so either can charge it. Store separately from harder gems to protect the polish. Avoid harsh chemicals and ultrasonic cleaners for fractured pieces. A soft cloth restores its shine.
identify: Genuine bloodstone is dark, nearly opaque green with irregular red spots and a waxy shine. Green jasper with painted-on red spots exists, and so does dyed chalcedony. Look for natural, uneven distribution of red; evenly spaced dots can be a sign of artificial work. Glass imitations show bubbles and chip with shell-like curves. The stone will scratch glass and feels cool and dense in hand.

faq.a: Bloodstone is traditionally used for courage, grounding, endurance and vitality. Crystal healers link it to the root and heart chakras and carry it when they need strength and steady resolve.
The name comes from the red iron-oxide spots on its dark green body, which resemble blood drops. Medieval legend also says it was created when Christ's blood stained green jasper beneath the cross.
Yes. Bloodstone is a traditional birthstone for March, sometimes listed alongside aquamarine. It has also been a classic gem for signet rings and seals.
